mainTopic: Liability of a בור for an ox that falls in (רב and שמואל on הבל and חבטה), and רבי נתן's rule for splitting payment between a pit owner and another cause of the damage
overview: The משנה taught that if an ox fell forward into a בור because of the noise of digging, the owner is liable, but if it fell backward, he is exempt. רב says both falls are into the pit, and the backward fall is exempt because the Torah makes a בור liable only for its bad air (הבל), not for the impact of the fall (חבטה). שמואל holds the owner liable for חבטה too. For him, the משנה's exempt case is an ox that tripped and landed behind the pit, outside it. A ברייתא that holds the owner liable even for a backward fall seems to refute רב, and רב חסדא, רבה and רב יוסף each give a different answer for him. רב חנניה then brings a ברייתא that supports רב. The גמרא asks why the pit owner is liable if the digging noise caused the fall, and answers that this follows רבי נתן: the pit owner pays whatever cannot be collected from the other cause. This leads into רבי נתן's ruling about an ox pushed into a pit, where the split is half and half for a מועד ox and a quarter and three-quarters for a תם ox, with two explanations of that split. Finally רבא applies the same dispute to a stone left at the opening of a pit, and a new teaching begins with איתמר.

steps.title: רב: Both the Forward and Backward Falls Are Inside the Pit
steps.stepSummary: רב finishes his explanation of the משנה: in both cases, forward and backward, the ox fell into the pit itself.
steps.simpleTranslation: And both this case and that case are talking about falling into the pit.
steps.whatsHappening: This line finishes רב's explanation of the משנה's two cases. He says both the 'forward' and the 'backward' falls happened inside the בור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רב, 'forward' and 'backward' describe how the ox landed (on its face or on its back), not where it landed. So the משנה's exemption for 'backward' applies even though the animal really fell into the pit. That raises the question of why the digger should be exempt, and the next step answers it.

keyTerms.meaning: This one and that one: both cases
A pit; one of the main categories of נזק
Because of the sound of the digging (the משנה's case)

steps.confusionAlert: Don't read 'backward' as 'behind the pit.' For רב, both falls are inside the pit. The only difference is whether the ox landed on its face or on its back.

phrases.english: And both this and that are in the pit.
phrases.notes: 'This and that' means the forward fall and the backward fall from the משנה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רב's explanation of the משנה, which began just before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Both cases in the משנה involve the ox falling into the pit itself; they differ only in how it landed.

steps.title: רב's Reasoning: Liability for Bad Air, Not Impact
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא shows that רב is consistent with his known view that בור makes one liable only for הבל (bad air), not for חבטה (the impact of the fall).
steps.simpleTranslation: רב follows his own reasoning. רב said: the בור that the Torah makes a person liable for covers damage from its bad air, not damage from the impact of the fall.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why רב exempts the backward fall. It points to another statement of רב: liability for בור is only for damage from the pit's air, not from the blow of hitting the ground.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An ox that falls on its face can breathe the pit's bad air and die from it, so the digger is liable. An ox that lands on its back is hurt by the impact, and רב holds there is no liability for חבטה. That is how רב explains the משנה's split between forward and backward.

keyTerms.meaning: Following his own reasoning; consistent with another view he holds
The pit's bad air or fumes
The blow or impact of falling and hitting the ground

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the basic question that splits רב and שמואל: what exactly is the harm that makes a בור owner liable?

phrases.english: Rav follows his own reasoning –
as Rav said:
the pit that the Torah made one liable for –
is for its fumes, and not for its impact.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the underlying principle that explains רב's reading in step 1.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The Torah's liability for בור covers death from הבל, not from חבטה.

steps.title: שמואל: Liable Whether It Falls Forward or Backward
steps.stepSummary: שמואל disagrees and holds the digger liable whenever the ox falls into the pit, whichever way it lands.
steps.simpleTranslation: And שמואל said: if it fell into the pit, whether forward or backward, he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל gives the opposing view. If the ox fell into the pit, the digger pays no matter how it landed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This goes directly against רב, who exempts the backward fall into the pit. It also creates a problem, because the משנה clearly exempts some backward fall. The גמרא will soon have to explain how שמואל reads that.

phrases.english: And Shmuel said:
In the pit – whether forward
or backward, he is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Presents the opposing opinion to רב.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Any fall into the pit, forward or backward, makes the digger liable.

steps.title: שמואל's Reasoning: Bad Air, and All the More So Impact
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא shows שמואל is consistent with his view that בור makes one liable for הבל, and all the more so for חבטה.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל follows his own reasoning, as he said: one is liable for its bad air, and all the more so for its impact.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains שמואל's view the same way it explained רב's. It points to another statement of his: liability for בור includes the bad air and, even more so, the impact.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For שמואל, the impact of the fall is an even more obvious harm than the air, so it is surely included. That is why a backward fall into the pit, which causes harm by impact, still makes the digger liable.
steps.whatToRemember: רב: a בור makes one liable only for הבל (bad air), not חבטה (impact). שמואל: liable for הבל, and all the more so for חבטה.

phrases.english: Shmuel follows his own reasoning, as he said:
for its fumes – and all the more so for its impact.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the principle behind שמואל's ruling in step 3, matching step 2 for רב.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Liability for בור covers הבל and, all the more so, חבטה.

steps.title: Then When Is a Backward Fall Exempt for שמואל?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges שמואל: if every fall into the pit makes one liable, what case does the משנה mean when it exempts a backward fall?
steps.simpleTranslation: But then what is the case of falling backward because of the sound of digging, where the משנה says he is exempt?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on שמואל using the משנה. If he holds the digger liable for every fall into the pit, the משנה's exemption for falling backward needs a case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה clearly gives an exemption for a backward fall. רב explained it easily, since impact is not covered. שמואל covers impact too, so he must find a different case where the משנה's exemption fits.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? How does it look?

phrases.english: But then what is the case of
backward because of the sound of digging – where he is exempt?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges שמואל's view (steps 3–4) from the wording of the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's ruling that any fall into the pit makes one liable
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה exempts a backward fall. If שמואל holds one liable even for impact inside the pit, that exemption seems to have no case to apply to.

steps.title: The Ox Tripped and Fell Behind the Pit, Outside It
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that according to שמואל, the משנה's exempt case is an ox that tripped on the pit and fell behind it, outside the pit.
steps.simpleTranslation: For example, where it tripped on the pit and fell behind the pit, outside the pit.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers for שמואל. 'Backward' in the משנה means the ox tripped over the pit and landed past it, outside the pit, so the pit itself did no damage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל reads 'backward' as describing where the ox landed, not how it landed. Since the ox never went into the pit, there is no damage from הבל or from חבטה inside the pit, and the digger is exempt. This keeps his rule that any fall into the pit makes the digger liable.
steps.whatToRemember: רב: 'backward' means the ox landed on its back inside the pit, and he is exempt because impact is not covered. שמואל: 'backward' means the ox landed behind the pit, outside it, and he is exempt because it never fell in.

phrases.english: For example, where it tripped on the pit,
and fell behind the pit, outside the pit.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 5.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case: 'backward' refers to where the ox landed, not how it landed
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה's backward fall is inside the pit, which would contradict שמואל.
steps.terutzMaskana: For שמואל, the משנה's exempt case is an ox that tripped and landed outside the pit, behind it.

steps.title: A ברייתא seems to refute רב
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא that holds the digger liable whether the ox fell forward or backward, which seems to contradict רב.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged him: A ברייתא says about a pit: whether the animal fell forward or backward, he is liable. This is a refutation of רב!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that says a pit makes one liable even when the ox falls backward. That seems to directly disprove רב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב said a backward fall means the ox died from the impact (חבטה), and a pit only makes one liable for its bad air (הבל). The ברייתא makes no difference between forward and backward, so it seems to hold the digger liable for חבטה too, just like שמואל.

keyTerms.meaning: They challenged him (usually from a ברייתא or משנה)
A refutation; a strong disproof of an opinion

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
With a pit, whether it fell forward
or whether it fell backward, he is liable.
This is a refutation of רב!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After defending שמואל in steps 5-6, the גמרא now turns to challenge רב.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's view that a pit makes one liable only for הבל, so a backward fall is exempt.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא holds the digger liable even for a backward fall, which by רב's logic is a death from חבטה, so it contradicts רב.

steps.title: רב חסדא: a pit on the digger's own property
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא answers that רב agrees the digger is liable for a backward fall when the pit is on his own property, because both the air and the ground belong to him.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said: רב agrees that with a pit in one's own property he is liable, because the ox owner can say to him: Whichever way you look at it, you are liable. If it died from the bad air, it is your bad air; if it died from the impact, it is your impact.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא saves רב by saying the ברייתא is talking about a pit dug in the digger's own property. In that case, even רב agrees he is liable either way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally רב exempts the impact because the ground the ox hits is not the digger's. But when the pit is in his own property, the ground is also his, so whether the ox died from the air or from the impact, it was his thing that killed it. That is why the ברייתא says he is liable even for a backward fall.

keyTerms.meaning: Whichever way you look at it; either way
The bad air of the pit
The impact of hitting the ground

phrases.english: רב חסדא said:
רב agrees about a pit on his own property that he is liable,
because the ox owner can say to him: Whichever way you look at it,

phrases.aramaic: אִי בְּהַבְלָא מִית – הַבְלָא דִּידָךְ הוּא,
phrases.english: if it died from the bad air, it is your bad air;

phrases.aramaic: אִי בְּחַבְטָא מִית – חַבְטָא דִּידָךְ הוּא.
phrases.english: if it died from the impact, it is your impact.
phrases.notes: Since the pit is on his land, the ground at the bottom that the ox hit belongs to him too.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא: מוֹדֶה רַב בְּבוֹר בִּרְשׁוּתוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 7 by limiting the ברייתא to a specific case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the ברייתא to a special case (a pit on private property) where רב agrees.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to speak of a normal pit, holding the digger liable for impact in general.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא speaks of a pit on the digger's own land, where both the air and the impact are his, so רב agrees he is liable.
steps.confusionAlert: רב חסדא is not saying רב changed his mind about the impact in general. רב still exempts the impact in a normal pit; only on the digger's own land is the impact counted as 'his'.

steps.title: רבה: the ox fell on its face and then flipped
steps.stepSummary: רבה answers that the ברייתא's 'backward' case is an ox that first fell on its face and then flipped onto its back, so the bad air already harmed it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: Here we are dealing with an ox that tumbled, that fell on its face, then flipped over and fell on its back. Since the bad air already took effect on it, it took effect on it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה gives a different way to fit the ברייתא with רב. He says the ox in the ברייתא started falling face-first and only then turned onto its back.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because the ox first fell facing down, it was already harmed by the pit's bad air before it flipped. So even though it ended up on its back, the הבל did its work, and רב can hold the digger liable for the הבל. This answer keeps the ברייתא in a normal pit, unlike רב חסדא.

keyTerms.meaning: Here, what case are we dealing with?

phrases.english: רבה said:
Here, what are we dealing with?
With one that tumbled, that fell on its face
and flipped over and fell on its back;
since the bad air that took effect on it, already took effect on it.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבָּה אָמַר: הָכָא בְּמַאי עָסְקִינַן – בְּמִתְהַפֵּךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, independent answer to the challenge of step 7.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the ברייתא's 'backward' case as a fall that began face-first.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Backward' meant the ox fell straight onto its back and died only from the impact.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ox first fell on its face and was hurt by the הבל, so the digger is liable for the הבל even by רב.

steps.title: רב יוסף: the ox damaged the pit
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף answers that the ברייתא is about an ox that damages the pit by fouling its water, so the ox owner is liable either way.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: Here we are dealing with damage to a pit caused by an ox. What is it? That it made the water foul. Then it makes no difference forward and no difference backward; he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף says the ברייתא is not about the pit hurting the ox at all. It is about the ox hurting the pit by spoiling its water, so the ox's owner must pay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once we read the ברייתא as the ox ruining the water, the direction of the fall does not matter: either way, the dead or fallen ox spoiled the water. So the ברייתא says nothing about liability for חבטה, and it does not contradict רב.

keyTerms.meaning: Damage to the pit caused by the ox

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא that seemed to refute רב is answered three ways: רב חסדא (the pit is on the digger's own land), רבה (the ox fell face-first and then flipped), and רב יוסף (the ox damaged the pit's water). In all three, רב's rule that a pit is liable for הבל and not for חבטה stays in place.

phrases.english: רב יוסף said:
Here we are dealing with damage to the pit by the ox.
What is it? That it made its water foul;
so it makes no difference forward
and no difference backward; he is liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב יוֹסֵף אָמַר: הָכָא בְּנִזְקֵי בוֹר בְּשׁוֹר עָסְקִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third, independent answer to the challenge of step 7.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reverses who is the damager: the ברייתא is about the ox damaging the pit.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא was about the pit's owner being liable for the ox that fell in.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא is about the ox's owner being liable for fouling the pit's water, which happens no matter how the ox fell.
steps.confusionAlert: Watch who is liable here. In this answer the 'he is liable' means the ox's owner pays the pit's owner, the opposite of the rest of the discussion.

steps.title: A ברייתא that supports רב: only a normal forward fall counts
steps.stepSummary: רב חנניה teaches a ברייתא that reads the word וְנָפַל as a normal fall. An animal that falls forward into a pit makes the owner liable, and one that falls backward does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חנניה taught a ברייתא that supports רב: 'And it fall' means the owner is not liable until the animal falls in the normal way of falling. From here they said: if it fell forward because of the sound of digging, he is liable; if it fell backward because of the sound of digging, he is exempt. In both cases it fell into the pit.
steps.whatsHappening: After all the answers to the challenge against רב, the גמרא now brings a ברייתא that openly supports רב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word וְנָפַל is read as 'falling the normal way,' which means falling forward. So a backward fall is exempt, exactly as רב said. The ברייתא stresses that both falls are into the pit, so it is clear that the only difference is the direction of the fall.

phrases.english: Rav Chananya taught in support of Rav:
"And it fall" means: not until it falls in the normal manner of falling.
From here they said:
If it fell forward because of the sound of the digging, he is liable,
if it fell backward because of the sound of the digging, he is exempt.
And both this one and that one fell into the pit.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the defenses of רב in Steps 8-10, brings a positive source that supports him
steps.raayaObject: רב's ruling that a backward fall into a pit is exempt
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא taught by רב חנניה that reads וְנָפַל as a normal forward fall

steps.title: Why is the pit owner liable if the digging noise caused the fall?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא questions the ברייתא's ruling. If the noise of digging scared the animal into the pit, why not blame the one who made the noise instead of the pit?
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: if it fell forward because of the sound of digging, he is liable. But why? Let us say the digger caused it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the ruling from the ברייתא it just brought and challenges it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The animal fell because the noise frightened it. That means the person digging caused the fall, not just the pit. So why should the pit make its owner liable?

keyTerms.meaning: 'The Master said', the formula for quoting a source that was just cited so it can be discussed

phrases.english: The Master said:
If it fell forward because of the sound of the digging, he is liable.
But why?
Let us say the digger caused it!

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר מָר נָפַל לְפָנָיו מִקּוֹל הַכְּרִיָּיה חַיָּיב וְאַמַּאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Analyzes the ברייתא just quoted in Step 11
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's ruling that a forward fall caused by the digging noise makes the pit owner liable
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The direct cause of the fall was the digger's noise, so the pit should not carry the liability

steps.title: The ברייתא follows רבי נתן: if one cause cannot pay, the other pays
steps.stepSummary: רב שימי בר אשי explains that the ברייתא follows רבי נתן. In his view the pit owner is a real damager, so when payment cannot be collected from the other cause, the pit owner pays.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב שימי בר אשי said: Whose opinion is this? It is רבי נתן, who says that the pit owner does damage, and wherever payment cannot be collected from this one, it is collected from that one.
steps.whatsHappening: רב שימי בר אשי answers the question by naming the תנא behind the ברייתא, רבי נתן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי נתן holds that the pit owner is himself a damager, not someone who is simply nearby when damage happens. So even when another cause played a part, if that cause cannot be made to pay, the pit owner covers the damage.

phrases.english: Rav Shimi bar Ashi said:
Whose opinion is this? It is Rabbi Natan,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר: בַּעַל הַבּוֹר הֶזֵּיקָא קָא עָבֵיד,
phrases.english: who says: the owner of the pit is doing damage,

phrases.aramaic: וְכֹל הֵיכָא דְּלָא אֶפְשָׁר לְאִשְׁתַּלּוֹמֵי מֵהַאי –
phrases.english: and anywhere that it is not possible to collect payment from this one,
payment is collected from that one;
phrases.notes: Here, 'this one' is the one whose noise scared the animal, and 'that one' is the owner of the pit.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב שִׁימִי בַּר אָשֵׁי הָא מַנִּי רַבִּי נָתָן הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 12
steps.terutzResolutionType: Attributing the ruling to a specific תנא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The digger's noise is the real cause, so the pit owner should be exempt
steps.terutzMaskana: According to רבי נתן, the pit owner pays whatever cannot be collected from the other cause

steps.title: The source for רבי נתן: an ox that pushed another ox into a pit
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא shows רבי נתן's view. The תנא קמא makes only the pushing ox's owner pay, while רבי נתן splits the payment in half between the ox owner and the pit owner.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is taught: An ox that pushed another ox into a pit: the ox's owner is liable and the pit's owner is exempt. רבי נתן says: the ox's owner pays half and the pit's owner pays half.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא as the source showing that רבי נתן holds the pit owner responsible even when another cause was involved.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תנא קמא puts all the blame on the ox that did the pushing. רבי נתן disagrees and holds the pit owner partly responsible as well. This proves he sees the pit owner as a real damager.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is taught in a ברייתא

phrases.english: As it is taught:
An ox that pushed another ox into a pit:

phrases.aramaic: בַּעַל הַשּׁוֹר חַיָּיב, בַּעַל הַבּוֹר פָּטוּר.
phrases.english: the owner of the ox is liable, the owner of the pit is exempt.
Rabbi Natan says:
the owner of the ox pays half,
and the owner of the pit pays half.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתַנְיָא שׁוֹר שֶׁדָּחַף אֶת חֲבֵירוֹ לְבוֹר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the source for the view of רבי נתן cited in Step 13
steps.raayaObject: רבי נתן's view that the pit owner is a damager who shares the payment with another cause
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about an ox that pushed another ox into a pit

steps.title: A different ברייתא gives רבי נתן a different split
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings another ברייתא in which רבי נתן says the pit owner pays three-quarters and the ox owner pays one-quarter. This contradicts the half-and-half ruling.
steps.simpleTranslation: But isn't it taught that רבי נתן says: the pit's owner pays three parts, and the ox's owner pays a quarter!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that two ברייתות report רבי נתן's ruling on the same case in two different ways.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In one ברייתא רבי נתן splits the payment evenly. In the other, the pit owner pays three-quarters. Both cannot be his exact ruling for the same case.

keyTerms.meaning: But isn't it taught? (introduces a contradicting ברייתא)

phrases.english: But isn't it taught that Rabbi Natan says:
the owner of the pit pays three parts,
phrases.notes: Three out of four parts, meaning three-quarters of the damage.

phrases.english: and the owner of the ox pays a quarter!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָתַנְיָא רַבִּי נָתָן אוֹמֵר בַּעַל הַבּוֹר מְשַׁלֵּם שְׁלֹשָׁה חֲלָקִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ברייתא of Step 14 with a contradicting ברייתא
steps.kashyaTarget: The report that רבי נתן splits the payment half and half
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Another ברייתא quotes רבי נתן as splitting the payment three-quarters and one-quarter in the same case

steps.title: One ruling is about a תם ox, the other about a מועד ox
steps.stepSummary: The two ברייתות are talking about different oxen. With a מועד ox, the payment is split half and half. With a תם ox, the ox owner pays a quarter and the pit owner pays three-quarters.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult: this one is about a תם ox, and that one is about a מועד ox.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא settles the contradiction by saying each ברייתא is about a different kind of ox.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a מועד ox, רבי נתן splits the payment half and half. With a תם ox, whose owner never pays more than half damages, the ox owner pays only a quarter and the pit owner pays three-quarters. Exactly how רבי נתן reaches that three-quarters figure is what the גמרא asks next, in step 17.

keyTerms.meaning: An ox with no history of goring, whose owner pays half damages
An ox that has been warned about, whose owner pays full damages

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי נתן, the pit owner is a real damager and shares the payment with the other cause. He pays half with a מועד ox and three-quarters with a תם ox. Steps 17–19 explain how the three-quarters figure is reached.

phrases.english: It is not difficult;
this one is about a tam ox, that one is about a mu'ad ox.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא הָא בְּתָם הָא בְּמוּעָד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the contradiction raised in Step 15
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two ברייתות give conflicting reports of רבי נתן's view
steps.terutzMaskana: Three-quarters and one-quarter applies to a תם ox; half and half applies to a מועד ox

steps.title: How can a quarter and three-quarters make sense with a תם ox?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tests two ways of seeing the case. Neither one produces רבי נתן's split of a quarter and three-quarters for a תם ox.
steps.simpleTranslation: And with a תם ox, what does רבי נתן hold? If he holds that each one, the ox and the pit, did all the damage, then each should pay half. And if he holds that each did half the damage, then the pit owner pays half, the ox owner pays a quarter, and the victim loses the remaining quarter. Either way, where does three-quarters come from?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ruling from step 16. It shows that neither way of dividing the damage gives the pit owner three-quarters.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Option one: if each caused all the damage, the תם owner owes half (the most a תם ever pays), and the pit owner owes the other half. That makes half and half. Option two: if each caused half, the pit owner pays his half, the תם owner pays half of his half (a quarter), and one quarter is left unpaid. Neither option gives three-quarters.

keyTerms.meaning: An ox with no history of goring; its owner pays only half the damage
He holds / he is of the opinion
Loses (the victim does not get this part)

phrases.english: And with a תם ox, what does he hold?
phrases.notes: "He" is רבי נתן. This asks about the תם case from step 16: a quarter for the ox owner, three-quarters for the pit owner.

phrases.aramaic: אִי קָסָבַר: הַאי כּוּלֵּיהּ הֶזֵּיקָא עֲבַד
phrases.english: If he holds: this one did all the damage
and that one did all the damage —
then this one should pay half,
and that one should pay half!

phrases.aramaic: וְאִי קָסָבַר: הַאי פַּלְגָא הֶזֵּיקָא עֲבַד,
phrases.english: And if he holds: this one did half the damage,
and that one did half the damage —
then the pit owner pays half
and the ox owner pays a quarter,
and the other quarter, he loses it?
phrases.notes: "He" here is the victim, whose ox was killed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the logic behind the תם split given in step 16.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי נתן's ruling that with a תם ox the pit owner pays three-quarters and the ox owner pays a quarter
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A two-sided challenge: if each caused all the damage, the split should be half and half; if each caused half, the split should be half and a quarter, with a quarter lost. Neither gives three-quarters.

steps.title: רבא: each did all the damage, but the partnership must help the ox owner
steps.stepSummary: רבא says each one did all the damage. The ox owner pays only a quarter because he can say that sharing the blame should reduce what he owes.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: רבי נתן is a judge who goes down to the depths of the law. Really, he holds that each one did all the damage. As for your question of why the split is not half and half: the ox owner can say to the pit owner, 'If I still pay my full half, what good did being your partner do me?'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers the challenge using the first option, that each one did all the damage. He explains why the ox owner still pays only a quarter.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Alone, the תם owner would owe half. Since he shares the blame with the pit, he argues that his half should be split between them, so he pays a quarter. The pit owner, who would owe the full amount alone, covers the remaining three-quarters.

keyTerms.meaning: Goes down to the depth of the law; sees the fine details of fairness
Really / in fact (keeps an earlier option and defends it)

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that when two damagers share the blame, each one's share can depend on what he would have owed alone, not only on a simple even split.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רָבָא: רַבִּי נָתָן דַּיָּינָא הוּא,
phrases.english: רבא said: רבי נתן is a judge,
and he goes down to the depth of the law;
really, he holds:
this one did all the damage,
and that one did all the damage;
and as for what is hard for you,
that this one should pay half and that one half,

phrases.aramaic: מִשּׁוּם דְּאָמַר לֵיהּ בַּעַל הַשּׁוֹר לְבַעַל הַבּוֹר:
phrases.english: it is because the ox owner says to the pit owner:
phrases.notes: Here the "ox owner" is the owner of the pushing תם ox, the one who caused the damage.

phrases.english: "My partnership with you, what did it help me?"
phrases.notes: He means: alone I would pay half anyway, so sharing the blame should cut that half in two, leaving me a quarter.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: רַבִּי נָתָן דַּיָּינָא הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the first side of the challenge in step 17.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Keeps the first option and adds a fairness argument by the ox owner
steps.terutzHavaAmina: If each did all the damage, the תם owner pays his full half and the pit owner pays the other half.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ox owner can claim that the partnership must reduce his half to a quarter. The pit owner, liable in full on his own, pays three-quarters.

steps.title: Second answer: each did half, and the victim collects the missing quarter from the pit owner
steps.stepSummary: Another answer says each one did half the damage. The victim collects the unpaid quarter from the pit owner, since the ox was found in his pit.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you want, say: really, he holds that each one did half the damage. As for your question that the pit owner pays half, the ox owner pays a quarter, and the last quarter is lost: the owner of the dead ox can say to the pit owner, 'I found my ox in your pit, so you killed it. Whatever I can collect from the other one, I will collect. Whatever I cannot collect from him, I will collect from you.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second answer using the other option, that each one did half the damage. It explains who covers the quarter that seemed to be lost.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The pit owner pays his half. The תם owner pays half of his half, which is a quarter. The quarter the תם owner does not pay is collected from the pit owner, because the victim's ox was found dead in his pit. This is רבי נתן's rule from step 13: when one damager cannot be made to pay, the pit owner covers it.

keyTerms.meaning: If you want, say (introduces another answer)
From that other one (the owner of the pushing ox)

steps.confusionAlert: In this answer, "בעל השור" is NOT the owner of the pushing ox from step 18. It is the owner of the ox that fell in and died, the victim.
steps.whatToRemember: For a תם ox, רבי נתן's quarter and three-quarters can be explained two ways. Either each did all the damage and the partnership lowers the ox owner's share (רבא), or each did half and the victim takes the unpaid quarter from the pit owner.

phrases.english: If you want, say: really, he holds:
this one did half the damage,
and that one did half the damage;
and as for what is hard for you:
the pit owner pays half
and the ox owner pays a quarter,
and he should lose the other quarter —

phrases.aramaic: מִשּׁוּם דַּאֲמַר לֵיהּ בַּעַל הַשּׁוֹר לְבַעַל הַבּוֹר:
phrases.english: it is because the ox owner says to the pit owner:
phrases.notes: This time the "ox owner" is the victim, whose ox died in the pit.

phrases.english: "I found my ox in your pit —
you killed it;
whatever I am able to collect from that one —
I collect,
whatever I am not able to collect from that one —
I collect from you."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different answer to step 17, defending the second option instead of the first.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Keeps the second option and fills the gap using רבי נתן's rule that the pit owner covers what cannot be collected elsewhere
steps.terutzHavaAmina: If each did half, the victim would lose the quarter the תם owner is not required to pay.
steps.terutzMaskana: The victim collects that missing quarter from the pit owner, since his ox was found dead in the pit. The pit owner pays three-quarters in total.

steps.title: A stone at the opening of a pit
steps.stepSummary: רבא says that if someone left a stone at the opening of another person's pit, and an ox tripped on it and fell in, this is the same case as the dispute between רבי נתן and the רבנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא says: If someone put a stone at the opening of a pit, and an ox came, tripped on it, and fell into the pit, we have reached the dispute of רבי נתן and the רבנן.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא brings a new case and says it follows the same dispute we just learned between רבי נתן and the רבנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the earlier case, an ox pushed another ox into a pit, so two causes worked together: the ox and the pit. Here the stone takes the place of the pushing ox. So the question of how to split the payment between the stone owner and the pit owner depends on the same dispute.

keyTerms.meaning: we have reached the dispute; this case depends on that argument

phrases.english: Rava says:
If one left a stone at the opening of a pit,
and an ox came and stumbled on it,
and fell into the pit –
we have arrived at the dispute of Rabbi Natan and the Rabbis.
phrases.notes: This is the dispute from earlier on the daf, about an ox that pushed another ox into a pit.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: הִנִּיחַ אֶבֶן עַל פִּי הַבּוֹר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the explanations of רבי נתן's payment split, רבא applies the same dispute to a new case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A stone left at a pit's opening that makes an ox fall in is judged by the same dispute between רבי נתן and the רבנן as an ox pushed into a pit.

steps.title: Isn't this obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רבא needed to say this, since the stone case looks just like the pushing ox case.
steps.simpleTranslation: That is obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבא's statement as too obvious to need saying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a pushing ox and a pit together cause the damage, a stone and a pit should work the same way. So what new thing is רבא teaching? This sets up the next step, which shows why it was not obvious.

keyTerms.meaning: It is obvious! (a challenge that a statement teaches nothing new)

phrases.english: It is obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבא's statement in step 20 as saying nothing new.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's statement that the stone case belongs to the dispute between רבי נתן and the רבנן
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The stone case seems identical to the pushing ox case, so there seems to be no need to state it.

steps.title: Why the stone owner can't escape blame
steps.stepSummary: We might have thought the stone owner could say his stone alone does no harm. רבא teaches that the pit owner can answer: without your stone, the ox would never have fallen in.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said: only there can the pit owner say to the ox owner, 'If not for my pit, your ox would have killed it anyway.' But here, the stone owner can say to the pit owner, 'If not for your pit, what would my stone have done? If the ox had tripped on it, it would have fallen and gotten up!' So רבא teaches us that the pit owner can answer him: 'If not for the stone, it would not have fallen into the pit.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why רבא's ruling was needed. The stone case has a special argument we might have accepted, and רבא rejects it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the ox case, the pushing ox could have killed the other ox by itself, so it was clearly a full cause of the damage. A stone by itself only makes an ox trip and get up, so we might think the pit did all the real damage and the stone owner is exempt. רבא teaches that the stone is still a real cause, because without it the ox never reaches the pit. So the same dispute applies.

keyTerms.meaning: You might have said (introduces a mistaken idea that the ruling comes to reject)
It teaches us (introduces the real lesson)
falls and gets up (no lasting harm)

steps.confusionAlert: Watch who is speaking to whom. In the first quote, the pit owner speaks to the ox owner (the old case). In the second, the stone owner speaks to the pit owner. In the last quote, the pit owner answers the stone owner.
steps.whatToRemember: A cause that does no harm by itself, like a stone that only makes an ox trip, still shares the blame if the damage would not have happened without it.

phrases.english: What might you have said?

phrases.aramaic: הָתָם הוּא דְּאָמַר בַּעַל הַבּוֹר לְבַעַל הַשּׁוֹר:
phrases.english: It is there that the owner of the pit can say to the owner of the ox:
phrases.notes: 'There' means the earlier case, where one ox pushed another into the pit.

phrases.english: "If not for my pit –
your ox would have killed it";
but here,

phrases.aramaic: מָצֵי אָמַר לֵיהּ בַּעַל אֶבֶן לְבַעַל הַבּוֹר:
phrases.english: the owner of the stone can say to the owner of the pit:
"If not for your pit,
what would my stone have done?
If it had stumbled on it –
it would have fallen and gotten up!"
It teaches us
that he can say to him:
phrases.notes: Here the pit owner is answering the stone owner.

phrases.english: "If not for the stone –
it would not have fallen into the pit."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'obvious' challenge of step 21 by showing an argument that makes the stone case different.
steps.terutzResolutionType: מהו דתימא / קא משמע לן: showing a mistaken idea the ruling comes to reject
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The stone owner is exempt, because his stone alone would only make the ox trip and get up, so the pit did all the real damage.
steps.terutzMaskana: The stone owner shares the blame, because without the stone the ox would not have fallen into the pit. So the case follows the dispute between רבי נתן and the רבנן.

steps.title: A new statement is introduced
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens with 'it was stated', getting ready to quote a new teaching of the אמוראים.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was stated:
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The גמרא is about to bring a new statement, and the next words will show what it is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word איתמר usually introduces a dispute or teaching of the אמוראים. Here it only opens the next topic and does not give any ruling yet.

keyTerms.meaning: It was stated (introduces a teaching or dispute of the אמוראים)

phrases.english: It was stated:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the discussion of רבא's stone case and opens a new statement.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: No ruling yet. This line introduces the next statement.
